[[Image:Von-Mises-Max-8x8.gif|thumb|right|Maximum von Mises stress in plane stress problem with the interval parameters (calculated by using gradient method).]]
In [[numerical analysis]], the '''interval finite element method''' ('''interval FEM''') is a [[finite element method]] that uses interval parameters. Interval FEM can be applied in situations where it is not possible to get reliable probabilistic characteristics of the structure. This is important in concrete structures, wood structures, geomechanics, composite structures, biomechanics and in many other areas.<ref name="apcie">{{Cite web |url=http://andrzej.pownuk.com/IntervalEquations.htm |title=Interval equations |access-date=2008-10-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111005092424/http://andrzej.pownuk.com/IntervalEquations.htm |archive-date=2011-10-05 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The goal of the Interval Finite Element is to find upper and lower bounds of different characteristics of the model (e.g. [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]], [[Displacement (vector)|displacements]], [[yield surface]] etc.) and use these results in the design process. This is so called worst case design, which is closely related to the [[limit state design]].

Worst case design requires less information than [[probabilistic design]] however the results are more conservative [Köylüoglu and [[Elishakoff]] 1998].{{Citation needed|date=January 2010}}

== Applications of the interval parameters to the modeling of uncertainty ==

Consider the following equation:
<math display="block"> ax=b </math>
where ''a'' and ''b'' are [[real number]]s, and <math> x = \frac{b}{a} </math>.

Very often, the exact values of the parameters ''a'' and ''b'' are unknown.

Let's assume that <math> a\in[1,2]=\mathbf{a} </math> and <math> b\in[1,4]=\mathbf{b} </math>. In this case, it is necessary to solve the following equation
<math display="block"> [1,2]x=[1,4] </math>

There are several definitions of the solution set of this equation with interval parameters.

=== United solution set ===

In this approach the solution is the following set
<math display="block"> \mathbf{x} = \left\{ x: ax=b, a\in\mathbf{a}, b\in\mathbf{b} \right\} = \frac{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{[1,4]}{[1,2]} = [0.5, 4] </math>

This is the most popular solution set of the interval equation and this solution set will be applied in this article.

In the multidimensional case the united solutions set is much more complicated.
The solution set of the following system of [[Interval arithmetic#Linear interval systems|linear interval equations]]
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
 {[-4,-3]} & {[-2,2]}\\
 {[-2,2]} & {[-4,-3]}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
{[-8,8]} \\
{[-8,8]}
\end{bmatrix}
</math>
is shown on the following picture
[[image:Solution_set.png|600px]]
<math display="block"> \sum{_{\exists\exists}}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{b})=\{x: Ax=b, A\in\mathbf{A},b\in\mathbf{b}\} </math>

The exact solution set is very complicated, thus it is necessary to find the smallest interval which contains the exact solution set
[[image:Solution-set-3.png|600px]]
<math display="block"> \diamondsuit\left(\sum{_{\exists\exists}}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{b})\right)=\diamondsuit\{x: Ax=b, A\in\mathbf{A},b\in\mathbf{b}\} </math>
or simply
<math display="block"> \diamondsuit\left(\sum{_{\exists\exists}}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{b})\right)=[\underline x_1,\overline x_1] \times [\underline x_2,\overline x_2] \times \dots \times [\underline x_n,\overline x_n] </math>
where
<math display="block"> \underline x_i=\min\{x_i: Ax=b, A\in\mathbf{A},b\in\mathbf{b}\}, \ \ \overline x_i = \max\{x_i: Ax=b, A\in\mathbf{A},b\in\mathbf{b}\} </math>
<math display="block"> x_i\in\{x_i: Ax=b, A\in\mathbf{A},b\in\mathbf{b}\}=[\underline x_i,\overline x_i] </math>
See also [http://www.ippt.gov.pl/~kros/pccmm99/01Title.html]

===Parametric solution set of interval linear system===

The Interval Finite Element Method requires the solution of a parameter-dependent system of equations (usually with a symmetric positive definite matrix.) An example of the solution set of general parameter dependent system of equations

<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
p_1 & p_2 \\
p_2 + 1 & p_1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{p_1+6p_2}{5.0} \\
2p_1-6
\end{bmatrix},
\ \ \text{for} \ \ p_1\in[2,4], p_2\in[-2,1].
</math>
is shown on the picture below.<ref>[http://cose.math.bas.bg/webMathematica/webComputing/ParametricSSet.jsp E. Popova, Parametric Solution Set of Interval Linear System] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100127132504/http://cose.math.bas.bg/webMathematica/webComputing/ParametricSSet.jsp |date=2010-01-27 }}</ref>

[[Image:Interval-equation.gif|Solution set of the parameter dependent system of equations]]

=== Algebraic solution ===

In this approach x is an [[Interval (mathematics)|interval number]] for which the equation
<math display="block"> [1,2]x=[1,4] </math>
is satisfied. In other words, the left side of the equation is equal to the right side of the equation.
In this particular case the solution is <math> x =[1,2] </math> because
<math display="block"> ax =[1,2][1,2]=[1,4] </math>

If the uncertainty is larger, i.e. <math> a=[1,4] </math>, then <math>x=[1,1]</math> because
<math display="block"> ax =[1,4][1,1]=[1,4] </math>

If the uncertainty is even larger, i.e. <math> a=[1,8] </math>, then the solution doesn't exist. It is very complex to find a physical interpretation of the algebraic interval solution set.
Thus, in applications, the united solution set is usually applied.

== The method ==

Consider the PDE with the interval parameters
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">G(x,u,p) = 0 </math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
where <math> p = (p_1,\dots,p_m) \in {\mathbf p} </math> is a vector of parameters which belong to given intervals
<math display="block">p_i\in[\underline p_i,\overline p_i]={\mathbf p}_i, </math>
<math display="block"> {\mathbf p} = {\mathbf p}_1\times {\mathbf p}_2 \times \cdots \times {\mathbf p}_m. </math>

For example, the heat transfer equation
<math display="block"> k_x \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}+ k_y\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} +q =0 \text{ for } x \in \Omega </math>
<math display="block"> u(x)=u^*(x) \text{ for } x \in \partial\Omega </math>
where <math> k_x, k_y </math> are the interval parameters (i.e. <math> k_x\in{\mathbf k}_x, \ k_y\in{\mathbf k}_y </math>).

Solution of the equation ({{EquationNote|1}}) can be defined in the following way
<math display="block"> \tilde{u}(x):= \{u(x): G(x,u,p) = 0,p\in {\mathbf p} \} </math>

For example, in the case of the heat transfer equation
<math display="block"> \tilde{u}(x) = \left\{ u(x) :k_x \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}+ k_y\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} +q =0 \text{ for } x \in \Omega , u(x)=u^*(x) \text{ for } x \in \partial\Omega, k_x\in{\mathbf k}_x, \ k_y\in{\mathbf k}_y \right\} </math>

Solution <math> \tilde {u} </math> is very complicated because of that in practice it is more interesting to find the smallest possible interval which contain the exact solution set <math>\tilde {u}</math>.

<math display="block"> {\mathbf u}(x)=\lozenge \tilde{u}(x) = \lozenge \{u(x):G(x,u,p)=0,p\in {\mathbf p} \} </math>

For example, in the case of the heat transfer equation
<math display="block"> {\mathbf u}(x) = \lozenge \left\{ u(x) :k_x \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}+ k_y\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} +q =0 \text{ for } x \in \Omega , u(x)=u^*(x) \text{ for } x \in \partial\Omega, k_x\in{\mathbf k}_x, \ k_y\in{\mathbf k}_y \right\} </math>

Finite element method lead to the following parameter dependent system of algebraic equations
<math display="block"> K(p) u = Q(p), \ \ \ p \in {\mathbf p} </math>
where {{mvar|K}} is a [[stiffness matrix]] and {{mvar|Q}} is a right hand side.

Interval solution can be defined as a multivalued function
<math display="block"> {\mathbf u} = \lozenge \{u:K(p)u = Q(p),p\in {\mathbf p}\} </math>

In the simplest case above system can be treat as a system of [[Interval arithmetic#Linear interval systems|linear interval equations]].

It is also possible to define the interval solution as a solution of the following optimization problem
<math display="block"> \underline u_i = \min \{u_i : K(p)u = Q(p), p\in {\mathbf p}\} </math>
<math display="block"> \overline u_i = \max \{u_i : K(p)u = Q(p), p\in {\mathbf p}\} </math>

In multidimensional case the interval solution can be written as
<math display="block"> \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}_1 \times \cdots \times \mathbf{u}_n = [\underline u_1,\overline u_1] \times \cdots\times [\underline u_n,\overline u_n] </math>

== Interval solution versus probabilistic solution ==

It is important to know that the interval parameters generate different results than [[Uniform distribution (continuous)|uniformly distributed random variables]].

Interval parameter <math> \mathbf{p}=[\underline p,\overline p] </math> take into account all possible probability distributions (for <math> p\in[\underline p,\overline p] </math>).

In order to define the interval parameter it is necessary to know only upper <math> \overline p </math> and lower bound <math> \underline p </math>.

Calculations of probabilistic characteristics require the knowledge of a lot of experimental results.

It is possible to show that the sum of n interval numbers is <math> \sqrt{n} </math> times wider than the sum of appropriate normally distributed random variables.

Sum of ''n'' interval number <math> \mathbf{p}= [\underline p,\overline p] </math> is equal to
<math display="block"> n\mathbf{p} = [n\underline p,n\overline p] </math>

Width of that interval is equal to
<math display="block"> n\overline p - n\underline p = n(\overline p - \underline p) = n\Delta p </math>

Consider [[Normal distribution|normally distributed random variable]] ''X'' such that
<math display="block"> m_X=E[X]=\frac{\overline p + \underline p }{2}, \sigma_X=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[X]}=\frac{\Delta p}{6} </math>

Sum of ''n'' normally distributed random variable is a normally distributed random variable with the following characteristics (see [[Six Sigma]])
<math display="block"> E[nX]=n\frac{\overline p + \underline p }{2}, \sigma_{nX}=\sqrt{n\operatorname{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{n}\sigma=\sqrt{n}\frac{\Delta p}{6} </math>

We can assume that the width of the probabilistic result is equal to 6 sigma (compare [[Six Sigma]]).
<math display="block"> 6\sigma_{nX}=6\sqrt{n}\frac{\Delta p}{6}=\sqrt{n}\Delta p </math>

Now we can compare the width of the interval result and the probabilistic result
<math display="block"> \frac{\text{width of }n\text{ intervals}}{\text{width of }n\text{ random variables}} = \frac{n\Delta p}{\sqrt{n}\Delta p} = \sqrt{n} </math>

Because of that the results of the interval finite element (or in general worst-case analysis) may be overestimated in comparison to the stochastic fem analysis (see also [[propagation of uncertainty]]).
However, in the case of nonprobabilistic uncertainty it is not possible to apply pure probabilistic methods.
Because probabilistic characteristic in that case are not known exactly ([[Elishakoff]] 2000).

It is possible to consider random (and fuzzy random variables) with the interval parameters (e.g. with the interval mean, variance etc.).
Some researchers use interval (fuzzy) measurements in statistical calculations (e.g. [http://www.cs.utep.edu/interval-comp/interval.02/fers.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100616145927/http://www.cs.utep.edu/interval-comp/interval.02/fers.pdf |date=2010-06-16 }}). As a results of such calculations we will get so called [[imprecise probability]].

[[Imprecise probability]] is understood in a very wide sense. It is used as a generic term to cover all mathematical models which measure chance or uncertainty without sharp numerical probabilities. It includes both qualitative (comparative probability, partial preference orderings, ...) and quantitative modes (interval probabilities, belief functions, upper and lower previsions, ...). Imprecise probability models are needed in inference problems where the relevant information is scarce, vague or conflicting, and in decision problems where preferences may also be incomplete [https://www.sipta.org/].

== Simple example: modeling tension, compression, strain, and stress) ==

[[image:TensionCompression.JPG|400px]]

=== 1-dimension example ===

In the [[tension (physics)|tension]]-[[compression (physics)|compression]] problem, the following [[equation]] shows the relationship between [[displacement (vector)|displacement]] {{mvar|u}} and [[force]] {{mvar|P}}:
<math display="block"> \frac{EA}{L}u = P </math>
where {{mvar|L}} is length, {{mvar|A}} is the area of a cross-section, and {{mvar|E}} is [[Young's modulus]].

If the Young's modulus and force are uncertain, then
<math display="block"> E\in[\underline E,\overline E], P\in[\underline P,\overline P] </math>

To find [[upper and lower bounds]] of the displacement {{mvar|u}}, calculate the following [[partial derivative]]s:
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial u}{\partial E} = \frac{-PL}{E^2A} < 0 </math>
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial u}{\partial P} = \frac{L}{EA} > 0 </math>

Calculate extreme values of the displacement as follows:
<math display="block"> \underline u = u(\overline E,\underline P) = \frac{\underline PL}{\overline EA} </math>
<math display="block"> \overline u = u(\underline E,\overline P) = \frac{\overline PL}{\underline EA} </math>

Calculate [[Strain (mechanics)|strain]] using following formula:
<math display="block"> \varepsilon = \frac{1}{L} u </math>

Calculate derivative of the strain using derivative from the displacements:
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial E} = \frac{1}{L} \frac{\partial u}{\partial E} = \frac{-P}{E^2A} < 0 </math>
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial P} = \frac{1}{L} \frac{\partial u}{\partial P} = \frac{1}{EA} > 0 </math>

Calculate extreme values of the displacement as follows:
<math display="block"> \underline \varepsilon = \varepsilon(\overline E,\underline P) = \frac{\underline P}{\overline EA} </math>
<math display="block"> \overline \varepsilon = \varepsilon(\underline E,\overline P) = \frac{\overline P}{\underline EA} </math>

It is also possible to calculate extreme values of strain using the displacements
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial u} = \frac{1}{L} > 0</math>
then
<math display="block"> \underline \varepsilon = \varepsilon(\underline u) = \frac{\underline P}{\overline EA} </math>
<math display="block"> \overline \varepsilon = \varepsilon(\overline u) = \frac{\overline P}{\underline EA} </math>

The same methodology can be applied to the [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]]
<math display="block"> \sigma = E \varepsilon </math>
then
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial E} = \varepsilon + E\frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial E} =\varepsilon + E\frac{1}{L} \frac{\partial u}{\partial E} = \frac{P}{EA} - \frac{P}{EA}= 0 </math>
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial P} = E\frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial P} = E\frac{1}{L} \frac{\partial u}{\partial P} = \frac{1}{A} >0 </math>
and
<math display="block"> \underline \sigma = \sigma (\underline P) = \frac{\underline P}{A} </math>
<math display="block"> \overline \sigma = \sigma (\overline P) = \frac{\overline P}{A} </math>

If we treat stress as a function of strain then
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial\varepsilon}=\frac{\partial }{\partial\varepsilon}(E\varepsilon)=E> 0</math>
then
<math display="block"> \underline \sigma = \sigma (\underline \varepsilon) =E\underline \varepsilon = \frac{\underline P}{A} </math>
<math display="block"> \overline \sigma = \sigma (\overline \varepsilon) = E\overline \varepsilon = \frac{\overline P}{A} </math>

Structure is safe if stress <math> \sigma </math> is smaller than a given value <math> \sigma_0 </math> i.e.,
<math display="block"> \sigma < \sigma_0 </math>
this condition is true if
<math display="block"> \overline \sigma < \sigma_0 </math>

After calculation we know that this relation is satisfied if
<math display="block"> \frac{\overline P}{A} < \sigma_0 </math>

The example is very simple but it shows the applications of the interval parameters in mechanics. Interval FEM use very similar methodology in multidimensional cases [Pownuk 2004].

However, in the multidimensional cases relation between the uncertain parameters and the solution is not always monotone. In those cases, more complicated optimization methods have to be applied.<ref name="apcie"/>

=== Multidimensional example ===
In the case of tension-[[compression (physical)|compression]] problem the equilibrium equation has the following form
<math display="block"> \frac{d}{dx}\left( EA\frac{du}{dx} \right)+n=0 </math>
where {{mvar|u}} is displacement, {{mvar|E}} is [[Young's modulus]], {{mvar|A}} is an area of cross-section, and {{mvar|n}} is a distributed load.
In order to get unique solution it is necessary to add appropriate boundary conditions e.g.
<math display="block"> u(0)=0 </math>
<math display="block">\left.\frac{du}{dx}\right|_{x = 0} EA = P </math>

If [[Young's modulus]] {{mvar|E}} and {{mvar|n}} are uncertain then the interval solution can be defined in the following way

<math display="block"> {\mathbf u}(x)=\left\{u(x):\frac{d}{dx} \left( EA\frac{du}{dx} \right) + n=0,u(0)=0,\frac{du(0)}{dx}EA=P,E\in[\underline E,\overline E],P\in[\underline P,\overline P] \right\} </math>

For each FEM element it is possible to multiply the equation by the test function {{mvar|v}}
<math display="block"> \int_{0}^{L^{e}} \left( \frac{d}{dx}\left( EA\frac{du}{dx} \right)+n \right)v=0 </math>
where <math> x \in [0,L^{(e)}]. </math>

After [[integration by parts]] we will get the equation in the weak form
<math display="block"> \int_{0}^{L^{(e)}} EA\frac{du}{dx} \frac{dv}{dx} dx = \int_{0}^{L^{(e)}} nv \, dx </math>
where <math> x\in[0,L^{(e)}]. </math>

Let's introduce a set of grid points <math> x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{Ne} </math>, where <math> Ne </math> is a number of elements, and linear shape functions for each FEM element
<math display="block"> N_1^{(e)}(x)=1-\frac{1-x_{0}^{(e)}}{x_{1}^{(e)}-x_{0}^{(e)}}, \ \ N_2^{(e)}(x) = \frac{1-x_{0}^{(e)}}{x_{1}^{(e)}-x_{0}^{(e)}}. </math>
where <math> x\in [x_{0}^{(e)}, x_{1}^{(e)}]. </math>

<math> x_{1}^{(e)} </math> left endpoint of the element, <math> x_{1}^{(e)} </math> left endpoint of the element number "e".
Approximate solution in the "e"-th element is a [[linear combination]] of the shape functions

<math display="block"> u^{(e)}_{h}(x) = u^{e}_1 N_1^{(e)}(x)+u^{e}_2 N_2^{(e)}(x), \ \ v^{(e)}_{h}(x) = u^{e}_1 N_1^{(e)}(x)+u^{e}_2 N_2^{(e)}(x) </math>

After substitution to the weak form of the equation we will get the following system of equations

<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{E^{(e)}A^{(e)}}{L^{(e)}} & -\frac{E^{(e)}A^{(e)}}{L^{(e)}} \\
-\frac{E^{(e)}A^{(e)}}{L^{(e)}} & \frac{E^{(e)}A^{(e)}}{L^{(e)}} \\
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} u^{(e)}_1 \\ u^{(e)}_2 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\int_{0}^{L^{(e)}} n N_1^{(e)}(x)dx \\
\int_{0}^{L^{(e)}} n N_2^{(e)}(x)dx
\end{bmatrix}
</math>
or in the matrix form
<math display="block"> K^{(e)} u^{(e)} = Q^{(e)} </math>

In order to assemble the global stiffness matrix it is necessary to consider an equilibrium equations in each node.
After that the equation has the following matrix form
<math display="block">K u = Q</math>
where
<math display="block">
K= \begin{bmatrix}
K_{11}^{(1)} & K_{12}^{(1)} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
K_{21}^{(1)} & K_{22}^{(1)}+K_{11}^{(2)} & K_{12}^{(2)} & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & K_{21}^{(2)} & K_{22}^{(2)}+K_{11}^{(3)} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & K_{22}^{(Ne-1)} + K_{11}^{(Ne)} & K_{11}^{(Ne)} \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & K_{21}^{(Ne)} & K_{22}^{(Ne)}
\end{bmatrix}
</math>
is the global stiffness matrix,
<math display="block">
u = \begin{bmatrix}
u_0 \\
u_1 \\
\vdots \\
u_{Ne} \\
\end{bmatrix}
</math>
is the solution vector,
<math display="block">
Q=\begin{bmatrix}
Q_0 \\
Q_1 \\
\vdots \\
Q_{Ne} \\
\end{bmatrix}
</math>
is the right hand side.

In the case of tension-compression problem

<math display="block">
K= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{E^{(1)}A^{(1)}}{L^{(1)}} & -\frac{E^{(1)}A^{(1)}}{L^{(1)}} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
-\frac{E^{(1)}A^{(1)}}{L^{(1)}} & \frac{E^{(1)}A^{(1)}}{L^{(1)}} + \frac{E^{(2)}A^{(2)}}{L^{(2)}} & -\frac{E^{(2)}A^{(2)}}{L^{(2)}} & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & -\frac{E^{(2)}A^{(2)}}{L^{(2)}} & \frac{E^{(2)}A^{(2)}}{L^{(2)}}+ \frac{E^{(3)}A^{(3)}}{L^{(3)}} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac{E^{(Ne-1)}A^{(Ne-1)}}{L^{(Ne-1)}} + \frac{E^{(Ne)}A^{(Ne)}}{L^{(Ne)}} & -\frac{E^{(Ne)}A^{(Ne)}}{L^{(Ne)}} \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & -\frac{E^{(Ne)}A^{(Ne)}}{L^{(Ne)}} & \frac{E^{(Ne)}A^{(Ne)}}{L^{(Ne)}}
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

If we neglect the distributed load {{mvar|n}}

<math display="block">
Q=
\begin{bmatrix}
R \\
0 \\
\vdots \\
0 \\
P \\
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

After taking into account the boundary conditions the stiffness matrix has the following form

<math display="block">
K=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & \frac{E^{(1)}A^{(1)}}{L^{(1)}} + \frac{E^{(2)}A^{(2)}}{L^{(2)}} & -\frac{E^{(2)}A^{(2)}}{L^{(2)}} & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & -\frac{E^{(2)}A^{(2)}}{L^{(2)}} & \frac{E^{(2)}A^{(2)}}{L^{(2)}} + \frac{E^{(3)}A^{(3)}}{L^{(3)}} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac{E^{(e-1)}A^{(e-1)}}{L^{(e-1)}} + \frac{E^{(e)}A^{(e)}}{L^{(e)}} & -\frac{E^{(e)}A^{(e)}}{L^{(e)}} \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & -\frac{E^{(e)}A^{(e)}}{L^{(e)}} & \frac{E^{(e)}A^{(e)}}{L^{(e)}}
\end{bmatrix} = K(E,A) = K{\left(E^{(1)}, \dots, E^{(Ne)}, A^{(1)}, \dots, A^{(Ne)}\right)}
</math>

Right-hand side has the following form

<math display="block">
Q=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
0 \\
\vdots \\
0 \\
P \\
\end{bmatrix} = Q(P)
</math>

Let's assume that Young's modulus {{mvar|E}}, area of cross-section {{mvar|A}} and the load {{mvar|P}} are uncertain and belong to some intervals
<math display="block"> E^{(e)} \in [\underline E^{(e)},\overline E^{(e)}] </math>
<math display="block"> A^{(e)} \in [\underline A^{(e)},\overline A^{(e)}] </math>
<math display="block"> P \in [\underline P,\overline P] </math>

The interval solution can be defined calculating the following way

<math display="block"> \mathbf u = \lozenge \left\{u : K(E,A)u=Q(P) ,E^{(e)} \in [\underline E^{(e)},\overline E^{(e)}], A^{(e)}
\in [\underline A^{(e)},\overline A^{(e)}] ,P\in[\underline P,\overline P] \right\} </math>

Calculation of the interval vector <math> {\mathbf u} </math> is in general [[NP-hard]], however in specific cases it is possible to calculate the solution which can be used in many engineering applications.

The results of the calculations are the interval displacements
<math display="block"> u_i \in [\underline u_i, \overline u_i] </math>

Let's assume that the displacements in the column have to be smaller than some given value (due to safety).
<math display="block"> u_i< u^{\max}_i </math>

The uncertain system is safe if the interval solution satisfy all safety conditions.

In this particular case
<math display="block"> u_i< u^{\max}_i, \ \ \ u_i\in [\underline u_i, \overline u_i] </math>
or simple
<math display="block"> \overline u_i< u^{\max}_i </math>

In postprocessing it is possible to calculate the interval stress, the interval strain and the interval [[Yield surface|limit state functions]] and use these values in the design process.

The interval finite element method can be applied to the solution of problems in which there is not enough information to create reliable probabilistic characteristic of the structures ([[Elishakoff]] 2000). Interval finite element method can be also applied in the theory of [[imprecise probability]].

== Endpoints combination method ==

It is possible to solve the equation <math> K(p)u(p)=Q(p) </math> for all possible combinations of endpoints of the interval <math> \hat p </math>. <br />
The list of all vertices of the interval <math> \hat p </math> can be written as <math> L=\{p^*_1,...,p^*_n\} </math>. <br />
Upper and lower bound of the solution can be calculated in the following way

<math display="block"> \underline u_i = \min\{u_i(p_k^*):K(p_k^*) u(p_k^*) =Q(p_k^*), p_k^*\in L\} </math>
<math display="block"> \overline u_i = \max\{u_i(p_k^*):K(p_k^*) u(p_k^*) =Q(p_k^*), p_k^*\in L\} </math>

Endpoints combination method gives solution which is usually exact; unfortunately the method has exponential computational complexity and cannot be applied to the problems with many interval parameters.<ref name="Neumaier1990">A. Neumaier, Interval methods for systems of equations, Cambridge University Press, New York, 1990</ref>

== Taylor expansion method ==

The function <math> u=u(p) </math> can be expanded by using [[Taylor series]].
In the simplest case the Taylor series use only linear approximation

<math display="block"> u_i(p) \approx u_i(p_0)+\sum_j\frac{\partial u(p_0)}{\partial p_j}\Delta p_j </math>

Upper and lower bound of the solution can be calculated by using the following formula

<math display="block"> \underline u_i \approx u_i(p_0)-\left|\sum_j\frac{\partial u(p_0)}{\partial p_j}\right|\Delta p_j </math>

<math display="block"> \overline u_i \approx u_i(p_0)+\left|\sum_j\frac{\partial u(p_0)}{\partial p_j}\right|\Delta p_j </math>

The method is very efficient however it is not very accurate.<br />
In order to improve accuracy it is possible to apply higher order Taylor expansion [Pownuk 2004].<br />
This approach can be also applied in the [[interval finite difference method]] and the [[interval boundary element method]].

== Gradient method ==

If the sign of the derivatives <math> \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial p_j} </math> is constant then the functions <math> u_i= u_i(p)</math> is monotone and the exact solution can be calculated very fast.

:if <math> \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial p_j} \ge 0 </math> then <math> p_i^{\min} = \underline p_i, \ p_i^{\max} = \overline p_i </math>

:if <math> \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial p_j} < 0 </math> then <math> p_i^{\min} = \overline p_i, \ p_i^{\max} = \underline p_i </math>

Extreme values of the solution can be calculated in the following way

<math display="block"> \underline u_i=u_i(p^{\min}), \ \overline u_i=u_i(p^{\max}) </math>

In many [[structural engineering]] applications the method gives exact solution. <br />
If the solution is not monotone the solution is usually reasonable. In order to improve accuracy of the method it is possible to apply monotonicity tests and higher order sensitivity analysis. The method can be applied to the solution of linear and nonlinear problems of [[computational mechanics]] [Pownuk 2004]. Applications of sensitivity analysis method to the solution of civil engineering problems can be found in the following paper [M.V. Rama Rao, A. Pownuk and I. Skalna 2008].<br />
This approach can be also applied in the [[interval finite difference method]] and the [[interval boundary element method]].

==Element by element method==

Muhanna and Mullen applied element by element formulation to the solution of finite element equation with the interval parameters.<ref name="MuhannaMullen2001">R.L. Muhanna, R.L. Mullen, Uncertainty in Mechanics Problems - Interval - Based Approach. Journal of Engineering Mechanics, Vol.127, No.6, 2001, 557-556</ref> Using that method it is possible to get the solution with guaranteed accuracy in the case of truss and frame structures.

==Perturbation methods==
The solution <math> u = u(p) </math> [[stiffness matrix]] <math> K = K(p) </math> and the load vector <math> Q = Q(p) </math> can be expanded by using [[perturbation theory]]. Perturbation theory lead to the approximate value of the interval solution.<ref name="QiuElishakoff1998">Z. Qiu and [[I. Elishakoff]], Antioptimization of structures with large uncertain but non-random parameters via interval analysis Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering, Volume 152, Issues 3-4, 24 January 1998, Pages 361-372</ref> The method is very efficient and can be applied to large problems of computational mechanics.

==Response surface method==
It is possible to approximate the solution <math> u = u(p) </math> by using [[Response surface methodology|response surface]]. Then it is possible to use the response surface to the get the interval solution.<ref name="Akpan2000">U.O. Akpan, T.S. Koko, I.R. Orisamolu, B.K. Gallant, Practical fuzzy finite element analysis of structures, Finite Elements in Analysis and Design, 38, pp.&nbsp;93–111, 2000.</ref> Using response surface method it is possible to solve very complex problem of computational mechanics.<ref name="Beer2008">M. Beer, Evaluation of Inconsistent Engineering data, The Third workshop on Reliable Engineering Computing (REC08) Georgia Institute of Technology, February 20–22, 2008, Savannah, Georgia, USA.</ref>

==Pure interval methods==
Several authors tried to apply pure interval methods to the solution of finite element problems with the interval parameters. In some cases it is possible to get very interesting results e.g. [Popova, Iankov, Bonev 2008]. However, in general the method generates very overestimated results.<ref name="KulpaPownukSkalna1998">[[Zenon Kulpa|Kulpa Z.]], Pownuk A., Skalna I., Analysis of linear mechanical structures with uncertainties by means of interval methods. Computer Assisted Mechanics and Engineering Sciences, vol. 5, 1998, pp.&nbsp;443–477</ref>

==Parametric interval systems==
Popova<ref name="Popova2001">E. Popova, On the Solution of Parametrised Linear Systems. W. Kraemer, J. Wolff von Gudenberg (Eds.): Scientific Computing, Validated Numerics, Interval Methods. Kluwer Acad. Publishers, 2001, pp.&nbsp;127–138.</ref> and Skalna<ref name="Skalna2006">I. Skalna, A Method for Outer Interval Solution of Systems of Linear Equations Depending Linearly on Interval Parameters, Reliable Computing, Volume 12, Number 2, April, 2006, pp.&nbsp;107–120</ref> introduced the methods for the solution of the [[system of linear equations]] in which the coefficients are linear combinations of interval parameters. In this case it is possible to get very accurate solution of the interval equations with guaranteed accuracy.
